name: Carla Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Anything you say is confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt. That's what my kids say, anyway. I run a dozer on the overburden at Banfield North, a big open-cut coal mine, which means I shift the rock and soil that sits on top of the coal so the diggers can get at it. Twelve-hour shifts, and I spend most of it shaping benches and cleaning up behind the excavators.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been in mining?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years in March. Before that my sister Leila and I ran a café on Station Road for fourteen years. When the big supermarket opened with its own coffee bar, we hung on for eighteen months and then sold the equipment and closed. My husband Tariq runs road crews for the council and he said, try the mine, they're training people. So at forty-one I learned to drive a dozer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that nobody complains to me about their latte. I like the crew, and I like going home with a proper pay packet; we've got a good bit put away now, more than we ever did with the café. What's hard is that I'm still slow. The trainer, a lovely old fella called Viv, keeps telling me to trust the blade, and I keep not trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, one less thing. I'm not online much, but at smoko I'd say something like, well, that's saved us a lot of worry. I wouldn't make a big thing of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be very relieved. I've done one big change already, and it nearly flattened me. I just want a few years to get good at this job and stop feeling like the new girl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different at all. Keep going to work, keep saving, maybe finally replace the kitchen benchtop that's been cracked for five years. I'd keep asking Viv for extra time on the dozer simulator so I get faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weight off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the last change nearly flattened you. What was that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Closing the café was the worst year of my life. I sold our coffee machine to a kid on the internet for less than we paid for the milk jug. Leila didn't speak for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a bit of AI saving time here and there touch your work at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not that I know of. There's a GPS screen in the cab that shows me the design, and I suppose that's computers, but I've never used one of those chat things. Tariq's tried to show me. I'm not interested.

S0.say: She'd say at smoko that it's one less thing to worry about and a relief, but wouldn't make a big deal of it online or at work.
S0.think: She'd be deeply relieved because her last big change, closing the café, nearly flattened her. She wants years to get good at the job.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, keeps saving, finally replaces the cracked kitchen benchtop, and asks her trainer for more simulator time to get faster.
S0.feel: Calm, like a weight has lifted.
S0.quote: I sold our coffee machine to a kid on the internet for less than we paid for the milk jug.
S0.fieldNote: Carla's whole response is shaped by the café closing two years ago. She sees stability as the prize. The story of selling the coffee machine cheaply to a stranger online carried a lot of buried grief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something sensible, like, we'll see how it goes, the company will need people for a while yet. I don't take sides much. Some of it's the companies and some of it's just how things go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. They already run remote dozers at some mines, a bloke at the pub told me. I'm the slowest dozer on the crew, so if they keep three of us, I know which three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work harder, to be honest. I'd get extra hours on the simulator. I'd move more into savings and drop the benchtop plan. If my job went, I'd look for a dozer spot at one of the other mines round here before I'd think about anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but that knot in the stomach that I remember from the café's last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider retraining for whatever new jobs appear, like operating from a control room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know I should say yes. But I've just retrained once, and I'm still not good at this. I'd only do it if there was no other dozer job anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't take sides. Who do you think should do something about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone a bit. The company should give notice and training, the government should check they do, and people like me should probably try harder than I'm planning to. I'm being honest there.

S1.say: She'd say people will see how it goes and the company will need workers for a while yet. She tends not to blame any one side.
S1.think: She's privately worried, knowing remote dozers exist and that she's the slowest on her crew, so she'd be cut first.
S1.do: Works harder and puts in extra simulator hours, moves more money into savings and drops the benchtop plan, and would look for dozer work at nearby mines before considering anything new.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a stomach knot she remembers from the café's last year.
S1.quote: I'm the slowest dozer on the crew, so if they keep three of us, I know which three.
S1.fieldNote: Carla's response to threat is to dig in and try harder at what she knows, not to change course. She's pragmatic about who should act and admits honestly that she should try harder than she plans to. Plenty of nearby mines is her main comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mess and nobody was ready, and I wouldn't pretend to know the answer. I'd probably say the government needs to help people while they sort it out. I wouldn't be at any protests though, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd lose this job, Tariq would probably lose his road crew too, and there'd be no other dozers to go to because they'd all be robots. That's two careers in four years, and I don't have a third one in me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything that isn't the mortgage, food or the kids. I'd talk to Leila about whether we could pool money, because her husband's got a small engineering shop. I'd stay at the mine right up until they told me to go, and take any payout. Then I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at three every morning, like I was before the café closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years' warning help you at all, compared with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, with money. I'd have two more years of mine pay in the bank. But I wouldn't learn something new in two years, not at my speed. I'd just be saving and dreading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nadia and Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, at first. Nadia's thirteen and she reads everything, she'd know before I said. I'd probably make her favourite dinner and say we're fine, and she'd look at me like she knew I was lying.

S2.say: She'd say it's a mess nobody was ready for and that government should help people through it, but she wouldn't join protests.
S2.think: She fears losing her job while her husband loses his road crew, with no other dozer jobs left. She doesn't feel she has a third career in her.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the mortgage, food and the kids, talks to her sister about pooling money, stays at the mine until told to leave, and takes any payout.
S2.feel: Alarmed, waking at three in the morning like before the café closed.
S2.quote: I'd probably make her favourite dinner and say we're fine, and she'd look at me like she knew I was lying.
S2.fieldNote: For Carla the two-year scenario reopens a recent wound: a second career gone in four years. Her savings buy time but she can't picture using it to learn something new. Leaning on her sister's family is her real safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people a fair go to sort themselves out, and that the companies and the government should meet halfway on helping. Pretty middle of the road. I'd say it at smoko and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use most of that time not doing much. That's the truth. I'd keep driving, keep saving and keep hoping it was slower than they said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every extra dollar on the mortgage, and maybe by 2031 we'd owe a lot less. I'd keep working at Banfield as long as there was a seat. In year three or four, if Tariq pushed me, I might look at a course, maybe bookkeeping, since I did the café accounts for fourteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it'd come and go. Some weeks I'd forget about it, then something on the news would bring it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might do bookkeeping. Wouldn't AI do that too by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. See, that's why I wouldn't bother. Every time I think of a plan B, somebody tells me a computer's already doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Viv, my trainer. He's sixty-one and he's been on dozers since before I was born. He'd just retire, I think, and the mine would lose everything in his head.

S3.say: She'd say five years gives people a fair go and that companies and government should meet halfway on helping, keeping it middle of the road.
S3.think: She privately admits she'd mostly carry on driving and saving and hope the change came slower than predicted.
S3.do: Puts every extra dollar on the mortgage, keeps working at the mine as long as possible, and might look at a bookkeeping course in year three or four if her husband pushes.
S3.feel: Anxious on and off, with weeks of forgetting broken by news.
S3.quote: Every time I think of a plan B, somebody tells me a computer's already doing it.
S3.fieldNote: Carla is frank about waiting it out, and doubts every plan B because AI might do it too. Her idea of bookkeeping draws on real café skills, but she talks herself out of it quickly. The mortgage is her main lever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and nobody can complain they weren't warned. I'd say the young ones especially should plan for it. I'd sound quite calm about it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years doesn't help me as much as people think. I'd still have to change one day, and I hate changing. It'd just be ten years of knowing it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and get the mortgage paid off by fifty or so. I'd help Nadia pick a course that isn't going to vanish, maybe nursing or a trade where you're in people's homes. And somewhere around year five I'd probably force myself into a course, because Tariq would make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. Ten years of a little worry instead of two years of a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people say more time is always better. Is that true for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the money, yes. For me, it's just a longer queue to the same door. I'm not someone who uses time well when I'm scared of the thing at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would actually get you to start a course earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone I knew did it first and said it was fine. If Leila did it with me. I did the café with her, maybe I'd do the next thing with her too.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty and nobody can complain they weren't warned, and that young people especially should plan ahead.
S4.think: She privately feels ten years doesn't help as much as people assume, because she'd still have to change and hates change. It means ten years of knowing.
S4.do: Keeps working to pay off the mortgage by about fifty, helps her daughter choose a course unlikely to vanish, and pushes herself into a course around year five.
S4.feel: Quietly anxious, a small worry spread over ten years.
S4.quote: For me, it's just a longer queue to the same door.
S4.fieldNote: Carla is the rare person who says more time doesn't really help her, because she wouldn't use it well. The money side clearly improves, though. Doing the next thing together with her sister, as with the café, is the one plan that sounded like it might actually happen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Tariq and I would both lose our jobs at once and there'd be nowhere to go. What would help is a decent payout from the mine, and some kind of course where they actually walk you through it slowly, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how tired people are. Not lazy, tired. I've already started again once at forty-one. People keep talking about reinventing yourself like it's a hobby.

headlineQuote: I've already started again once at forty-one. People keep talking about reinventing yourself like it's a hobby.
portrait: Carla Rahman is a 43-year-old dozer operator at an open-cut coal mine, two years in after she and her sister closed their café of fourteen years. She's married to a council road-crew supervisor, has two kids and solid savings, and has never used an AI tool. She's pragmatic and middle of the road, blaming no one side, but she resists change and is still recovering from the last one. She is calm if AI fizzles and anxious or alarmed in every other picture, saying extra time mostly means a longer wait for a change she dreads.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she and her husband would both lose their jobs at once with nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: A decent payout from the mine and a slow, hands-on course with real people walking her through it, not a website.
